citation: Sharma, Kshitij, Michail Giannakos, and Pierre Dillenbourg. "Eye-Tracking and Artificial Intelligence to Enhance Motivation and Learning." Smart Learning Environments 7, no. 1 (2020): 13. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-020-00122-x.
discipline: computer science / learning analytics, HCI-adjacent -- eye-tracking-instrumented experiment combined with a deep-learning/regression prediction pipeline for MOOC motivation and learning
thesis: Sharma, Giannakos, and Dillenbourg address a stated evidentiary gap in MOOC learning analytics: click-stream, keystroke, and other interaction-log variables 'do not always capture users' learning and behavior (e.g., passive video watching).' The paper poses two research questions: (1) how eye-tracking behaviour mediates the relationship between students' motivation and their learning within a MOOC, and (2) how well learning gain and motivation can be predicted from eye-tracking data in its most basic form. To answer the first, the authors define a family of stimulus-derived gaze variables -- content coverage, scanpath-based variables (AOI misses, AOI backtracks), and 'with-me-ness' (perceptual and conceptual) -- and test each as a mediator between a validated motivation questionnaire (predictor, SPQ) and post-video quiz performance (outcome), using Baron and Kenny's (1986) three-step mediation procedure. To answer the second, the authors extract deep-learning features from per-slide gaze heat-maps via a pretrained VGG-19 convolutional network, reduce dimensionality with LASSO, and benchmark five regression algorithms (Gaussian Process, SVM, Random Forest, GAM) for predicting both learning and motivation scores, achieving best errors of 5.04% (learning) and 9.04% (motivation) NRMSE. Boredom is never named anywhere in the paper (confirmed by direct text search); the operative affective-motivational vocabulary is exclusively 'motivation' (deep/surface) and 'with-me-ness' (gaze-based teacher-student co-attention), both original constructs this entry treats as adjacent/analogical to the cluster's boredom vocabulary rather than as direct engagement with it.

sections.title: Abstract and keywords
sections.summary: States the MOOC-analytics gap (click-stream/keystroke variables miss passive video watching), previews the with-me-ness/gaze-variable framework and the AI prediction method, reports the headline result (learning predicted within ~5% error).

sections.title: 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates gaze-based measurement over click-stream analytics; surveys prior academic-performance predictors (prior grades, motivation/effort, socioeconomic status, schooling quality, attention, participation); states the two research questions and the perceptual/conceptual with-me-ness distinction.

sections.title: Related work -- Video based learning; Eye-tracking and education
sections.summary: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer & Moreno) and cue-summation theory (Paivio; Severin) frame prior video-modality comparisons (Tobagi; Cennamo, Savenye & Smith; Choi & Johnson); Prieto et al.'s teacher-orchestration-load eye-tracking and individual (Kizilcec et al.)/collaborative (Sharma et al. 2015a/b) online-learning eye-tracking lead into the eye-mind hypothesis (Just & Carpenter 1980), the paper's foundational warrant for treating gaze as an attention proxy.

sections.title: Methodology -- Participants and procedure
sections.summary: N=40 (12 female) university students, eligibility = prior completion of an introductory Java course; SMI RED 250 eye-tracker; two 'Functional Programming Principles in Scala' MOOC videos; SPQ before viewing, quiz after; sample-size justified against two systematic reviews spanning 85 eye-tracking studies (84.71% used 8-60 participants).

sections.title: Methodology -- Measures
sections.summary: Four gaze-variable levels of increasing semantic dependency (Table 1): content coverage (low, stimulus-only); scanpath variables (medium, AOI-dependent: misses, backtracks); perceptual with-me-ness (high, AOI + teacher deictic gestures); conceptual with-me-ness (highest, AOI + teacher dialogue); plus motivation (SPQ) and learning (post-video quiz).

sections.title: Methodology -- Data analysis
sections.summary: Mediation analysis (Baron & Kenny 1986); feature extraction for prediction (heat-map -> VGG-19 -> 1,000 features/slide -> sliding-window reduction to 100); LASSO feature selection (Tibshirani 1996, 10-fold CV); five regression algorithms benchmarked via 80/20 train-test split (32/8 students) with 5-fold CV, evaluated by NRMSE (Pelanek 2015).

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: Separate mediation results for content coverage (full mediation), scanpath variables (partial mediation, both AOI misses and backtracks), and with-me-ness (full mediation, both perceptual and conceptual) (Table 2); prediction results (Fig.11): best learning-prediction error 5.04% and best motivation-prediction error 9.04%, both Gaussian Process with polynomial kernel.

sections.title: Discussions and conclusions; Abbreviations/acknowledgements/references
sections.summary: Interprets each mediation result against prior reading-time/rereading literature; situates conceptual with-me-ness within grounding theory (Dillenbourg & Traum 2006); discusses real-time computability of each gaze variable; states future-work plans (pair problem-solving stimuli, novice comparisons, gaze-aware adaptive feedback); Norwegian Research Council funding; no participant data shared due to re-identification risk.

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: mapped (this entry's own extension) onto the paper's 'motivation' construct (deep vs. surface, via SPQ) paired with 'with-me-ness' as an operationalized attention/co-attention measure; deep motivation defined as 'intrinsic motivation towards learning,' surface motivation as 'fear of failing in the tests' -- the paper itself never uses 'engagement' or 'flow'

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: mapped (this entry's own extension) onto the AOI-miss scanpath variable, defined as a participant who 'did not look at that particular AOI at all during the period the AOI was present on the screen,' glossed as 'completely ignoring some parts of the slides'; no attention-failure or meta-awareness literature (e.g., Eastwood, Fisher/Hamilton) is cited by the source itself

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: thin/tangential: the Introduction's opening complaint that click-stream analytics fail to capture 'passive video watching' gestures at a low-engagement viewing mode adjacent to monotonous consumption, but the paper never develops this as a construct, offers no induction method, and does not measure it directly

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: not treated; the SPQ motivation measure is a validated approach-to-learning instrument (deep/surface), not a boredom state/trait measure, and is never framed as either

measures.label: gaze variance / fixation dispersion
measures.signal: gaze position (x,y), fixations, and saccades sampled at 250 Hz
measures.apparatus: SMI RED 250 remote eye-tracker; content coverage via per-10-second-slice heat maps (image-subtraction + connected-components 'attention point' extraction); scanpath variables via AOI definitions (misses, backtracks)
measures.keyResult: content coverage fully mediates motivation->learning (Table 2, row 1); AOI misses and AOI backtracks each partially mediate motivation->learning (Table 2, rows 2-3); good performers/high-motivation students show fewer misses, more backtracks, more coverage than poor performers/low-motivation students

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.signal: 10-item, 5-point Likert Study Process Questionnaire (5 deep-motivation items, 5 surface-motivation items)
measures.apparatus: Biggs, Kember & Leung (2001) Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ), paper/on-screen administration prior to video viewing
measures.keyResult: mean motivation 2.10 (SD=1.20); used as the predictor variable in every mediation model and as one of two machine-learning prediction targets

measures.label: behavioral (RT / errors / performance-monitoring)
measures.apparatus: instructor-validated, Coursera-style 10-question quiz administered after each of two MOOC videos
measures.keyResult: mean learning score 6.9/10 (SD=1.6); used as the outcome variable in every mediation model and as the second machine-learning prediction target

measures.label: ML classification
measures.signal: per-slide gaze heat-map images converted to a reduced deep-feature vector
measures.apparatus: pretrained VGG-19 CNN (Simonyan & Zisserman 2014) extracts 1,000 features/slide; non-overlapping sliding window (size 10) reduces to 100 features; LASSO (Tibshirani 1996, 10-fold CV) performs final feature selection; five algorithms benchmarked (Gaussian Process linear/polynomial, SVM linear/polynomial, Random Forest, GAM)
measures.sampleN: 40 (32 train / 8 test, 5-fold CV on training set)
measures.keyResult: best learning-prediction error 5.04% NRMSE (SD=0.52%, Gaussian Process polynomial kernel; 'less than one question' on the 10-item scale); best motivation-prediction error 9.04% NRMSE (SD=0.56%, same algorithm); note these are continuous-score regressions, not discrete classifiers, though 'ML classification' is this cluster's nearest controlled-vocabulary label

readings.claim: Content coverage fully mediates the motivation->learning relationship: motivation significantly predicts both content coverage and learning, but the direct motivation->learning path becomes non-significant once content coverage is added as a covariate.

AOI misses and AOI backtracks each only partially mediate motivation->learning: both scanpath variables are significantly predicted by motivation and significantly predict learning, but the direct motivation->learning path remains significant with the mediator included.
Perceptual and conceptual with-me-ness each fully mediate motivation->learning; conceptual with-me-ness shows a larger percentage-mediation effect than perceptual (39% vs. 33%).

Good performers with high motivation show significantly fewer AOI misses, significantly more AOI backtracks, and greater content coverage/reading time than poor performers with low motivation, directly contradicting Byrne, Freebody, and Gates's (1992) finding that the best readers are the fastest.
readings.stance: contests (a prior finding in the reading-time-and-performance literature)

readings.claim: Conceptual with-me-ness correlates with test score at r=0.36 (p<0.05), read as support for treating it as a gaze-based measure of a student's effort to sustain common ground with the teacher.
readings.stance: asserts, interpreted via Dillenbourg & Traum's grounding theory

readings.claim: Best learning-score prediction achieved 5.04% NRMSE using Gaussian Process with a polynomial kernel; best motivation-score prediction achieved 9.04% NRMSE with the same algorithm/kernel.

Content coverage and scanpath variables are real-time/low-preprocessing computable; perceptual with-me-ness would need computer-vision gesture detection to be automated; conceptual with-me-ness requires manual dialogue transcription, making it the least ready of the four variables for real-time adaptive feedback.

concepts.term: Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ, Biggs et al. 2001)
LASSO (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator)
Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer & Moreno)

interlocutors.name: Biggs, J., Kember, D., & Leung, D.Y. (2001) -- The revised two-factor Study Process Questionnaire (R-SPQ-2F)
interlocutors.role: source of the deep/surface motivation instrument used as the predictor variable throughout

interlocutors.name: Baron, R.M., & Kenny, D.A. (1986)
interlocutors.role: mediation-analysis procedure applied to every gaze variable tested against motivation and learning

interlocutors.name: Just, M.A., & Carpenter, P.A. (1980) -- A theory of reading: From eye fixations to comprehension
interlocutors.role: the eye-mind hypothesis, foundational warrant for treating gaze as an attention proxy; also quoted to caution against a single mode of reading

interlocutors.name: Sharma, K., Jermann, P., & Dillenbourg, P. (2014) -- 'With-me-ness': A gaze-measure for students' attention in MOOCs
interlocutors.role: self-citation; original definition of with-me-ness as a gaze measure correlated with learning gains, extended in this paper to include motivation as predictor and learning as mediated outcome

interlocutors.name: Sharma, K., Caballero, D., Verma, H., Jermann, P., & Dillenbourg, P. (2015a, 2015b)
interlocutors.role: self-citations; collaborative/joint-attention eye-tracking in MOOC and pair-programming contexts

interlocutors.name: Simonyan, K., & Zisserman, A. (2014) -- Very deep convolutional networks (VGG-19)
interlocutors.role: pretrained CNN architecture used for heat-map feature extraction in the prediction pipeline

interlocutors.name: Tibshirani, R. (1996) -- Regression shrinkage and selection via the lasso
interlocutors.role: LASSO feature-selection method applied after VGG-19 feature extraction

interlocutors.name: Dillenbourg, P., & Traum, D. (2006) -- Sharing solutions: Persistence and grounding in multimodal collaborative problem solving
interlocutors.role: grounding theory used to interpret conceptual with-me-ness as sustained common ground between student and teacher

interlocutors.name: Jermann, P., & Nussli, M.A. (2012)
interlocutors.role: supporting finding: better-performing pairs show more recurrent gaze patterns during deictic reference, cited in support of the perceptual with-me-ness result

interlocutors.name: Byrne, B., Freebody, P., & Gates, A. (1992)
interlocutors.role: prior finding (best readers are fastest readers) that this paper's own reading-time result contradicts

interlocutors.name: Reinking, D. (1988)
interlocutors.role: prior finding of no relation between comprehension and reading time, cited alongside Byrne et al. as part of an unresolved reading-time-performance literature

interlocutors.name: Millis, K.K., & King, A. (2001); Dowhower, S.L. (1987)
interlocutors.role: prior findings that literal rereading improves comprehension, explicitly distinguished by the authors from the AOI-backtrack construct (which is not literal rereading)

interlocutors.name: Kizilcec, R.F., Papadopoulos, K., & Sritanyaratana, L. (2014)
interlocutors.role: video-instruction design study (showing face on screen) cited as a design-implication touchpoint for gaze-informed MOOC video design

interlocutors.name: Prieto, L.P., Sharma, K., Dillenbourg, P., & Jesus, M. (2016)
interlocutors.role: teaching-analytics/orchestration-load eye-tracking study, cited as prior evidence of eye-tracking's value in educational settings

interlocutors.name: Pelanek, R. (2015)
interlocutors.role: source of the NRMSE metric used to evaluate all prediction results

tensions.axis: reading time/content coverage as a positive performance signal (this paper's finding) vs. reading speed as the positive performance signal (Byrne, Freebody & Gates 1992)
tensions.note: Sharma et al. find that good performers with high motivation had greater content coverage/reading time, the inverse of Byrne et al.'s finding that the fastest readers perform best; the authors resolve the tension only by invoking Just & Carpenter's caution that 'there is no single mode of reading,' not by adjudicating between the two findings.

tensions.axis: AOI backtracking (this paper's construct) vs. literal text rereading (Millis & King 2001; Dowhower 1987)
tensions.note: the authors explicitly flag that their AOI-backtrack measure is conceptually different from the rereading construct in the cited literature, since students refer back to already-visible slide content rather than rereading previously completed material, cautioning that the rereading-comprehension literature's findings should be applied only cautiously to their own backtrack result.

tensions.axis: real-time computability across the four gaze variables (engineering-readiness gradient)
tensions.note: the authors themselves rank their four constructs by real-time deployability: content coverage and scanpath variables are already real-time-ready, perceptual with-me-ness would need computer-vision automation, and conceptual with-me-ness is bottlenecked by manual dialogue transcription -- an internal tension between the paper's four gaze variables' theoretical value and their practical deployability in an adaptive feedback system.

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- eye-tracking channel
dataset_channels.note: Sharma et al.'s four-level gaze-variable framework (content coverage, scanpath/AOI variables, perceptual and conceptual with-me-ness) offers a plausible methodological template for a future VR attention study's eye-tracking channel, particularly the AOI-based attention/co-attention logic, but a VR headset's integrated eye tracking differs substantially in geometry (3D gaze vectors, headset-relative AOIs, no external teacher-deixis channel) from this study's 2D screen-based, teacher-video paradigm; linkage requires the dataset entry's own instrumentation to be confirmed (P/anticipatory-application).

dataset_channels.target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- ML/predictive-analytics channel
dataset_channels.note: The VGG-19-heat-map-feature-extraction + LASSO + Gaussian-Process/SVM/Random-Forest/GAM regression pipeline offers a concrete engineering template for a future automated engagement/boredom-scoring layer built on VR gaze data, but this is unconfirmed until the dataset entry specifies its own instrumentation and whether it would attempt an analogous AI-prediction layer at all (P/anticipatory-application).
